question: On routine stool examination of a 5-year-old with diarrhoea, you see oval cysts with 4 nuclei on iodine preparation. The mother reports the child passes pale, bulky, foul-smelling stools. What is the most likely organism?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Giardia lamblia cysts are oval with 4 nuclei visible on iodine staining. Giardiasis causes malabsorption with pale, bulky, steatorrhoeic stools due to villous damage and disruption of fat absorption in the duodenum and jejunum.

E. histolytica cysts can have 1–4 nuclei but are spherical (not oval) and typically present with dysentery (bloody mucoid stools), not malabsorption with pale fatty stools. The clinical picture of steatorrhoea points to a small-intestinal pathogen.

Cryptosporidium oocysts are much smaller (4–6 µm) and require modified ZN staining for identification — they are not seen on routine iodine preparation. Cryptosporidiosis causes profuse watery diarrhoea, especially in immunocompromised patients.

Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan pathogen; its cysts are large and spherical with a prominent macronucleus. It causes large-intestinal disease (dysentery), not small-intestinal malabsorption with steatorrhoea.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of oval cysts with 4 nuclei (on iodine prep) and steatorrhoeic stools (pale, bulky, foul-smelling) is classic for Giardia lamblia. Remember: Giardia affects the small intestine (malabsorption), while Entamoeba and Balantidium affect the large intestine (dysentery).

Oval cysts with 4 nuclei + malabsorption (pale, bulky, fatty stools) = Giardia lamblia. It colonises the duodenum and jejunum, causing villous atrophy and fat malabsorption. This is one of the most common parasitic causes of chronic diarrhoea in Indian children.
